rows.label: Concept
rows.text: All stoichiometric calculations follow one algorithm: **balance the equation, convert to moles, apply the coefficient ratio, convert to the required unit**. Mass uses n = m/M; gas volume at STP uses 22.4 L/mol; particles use Nₐ; solutions use molarity M = n/V(L) (mol per litre of solution, temperature-dependent) rather than molality (mol per kg solvent, temperature-independent).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - M = n/V(L) (molarity) - m = molality = n solute/kg solvent - M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (dilution) - M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ (titration, coefficients n)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: STP Definition: Standard Temperature and Pressure = 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm (101.325 kPa). Molar volume 22.4 L applies ONLY at STP. At other conditions use PV = nRT.  ·  Ideal Gas Assumption: Molar volume and simple gas stoichiometry assume ideal behavior. Real gases deviate at high pressure or low temperature.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Balanced chemical equations give mole ratios, not mass ratios."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***4 g NaOH in 250 mL*** — 0.1 mol in 0.25 L = 0.4 M (NEB 2024): the standard molarity question.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Molarity vs molality:** M = mol/L *solution*; m = mol/kg *solvent*. Only molality ignores temperature.  ·  **Dilution:** M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ conserves moles of solute — volumes are additive only approximately, moles exactly.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Every Calculation Is a Mole Hop Mass–mass, mass–volume, mass–particles, solution concentration — all stoichiometric calculations follow one route: **convert the given quantity to moles, apply the equation's mole ratio, convert to the required quantity**. Master the hop and every numerical becomes bookkeeping.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The universal algorithm 1. Write the **balanced equation**. 2. Convert the given quantity to **moles** (÷M for mass, ÷22.4 for gas volume at STP, ÷Nₐ for particles, ×V(L) for molarity). 3. Multiply by the **mole ratio** (coefficients). 4. Convert moles of the required species to the asked unit (×M, ×22.4, ×Nₐ, ÷V).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Balance → moles → ratio → unit. Write the four steps and NEB gives method marks even if arithmetic slips."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2024 (2m): 4 g of NaOH is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. Calculate its molarity. (NaOH = 40)** — n = 4/40 = 0.1 mol; V = 0.25 L; M = 0.1/0.25 = **0.4 M**.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: State units at every step — lost units are the top cause of lost marks in numericals.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Mole ratio from coefficients** — the only legitimate bridge between substances in a numerical.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Algorithm: balance → moles → ratio → convert. Molarity M = n/V(L). Mass–mass uses M; gas volumes use 22.4 L at STP; particles use Nₐ.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Every stoichiometry numerical, from Class 11 to industrial engineering, is the same four-step hop.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Number of moles in 36 g water is: → B  ·  Volume of 1 mol gas at STP is: → B

rows.text: ## 3. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Balanced Equation Required: All stoichiometric calculations must start with a correctly balanced chemical equation. Unbalanced equations give wrong mole ratios.  ·  Consistent Units: Always convert to moles first, then to target units. Mixing grams and liters without conversion causes errors.  ·  Verified PYQ 2024 (2m): molarity of 4 g NaOH in 250 mL = 0.4 M.
